overview.title: Why ConvNets, and a first small ConvNet (Listing 8.1)
overview.main_topic: The adoption history of deep learning in computer vision, the chapter's focus on small datasets, and Listing 8.1: a small Functional-API ConvNet for MNIST built from Conv2D and MaxPooling2D layers.
overview.central_idea: Deep learning overcame years of skepticism to dominate computer vision by 2016 and now powers everyday vision products. A ConvNet is a stack of Conv2D and MaxPooling2D layers; even a basic one will greatly outperform the 97.8%-accurate dense MNIST model of chapter 2.

summary:
The page completes the historical introduction begun on p.255. The computer vision community had invested for years in methods other than neural networks and was not ready to drop them for "a new kid on the block." In 2013 and 2014 deep learning still faced intense skepticism from many senior researchers; it only became **dominant in 2016**. One author recalls urging an ex-professor in February 2014 to pivot to deep learning ("It's the next big thing!" / "Well, maybe it's just a fad"); by 2016 that whole lab was doing deep learning.

Today, deep learning vision models are everywhere: Google Photos, Google image search, phone cameras, YouTube, OCR software, and research in autonomous driving, robotics, AI-assisted medical diagnosis, autonomous retail checkout and autonomous farming. The chapter introduces **convolutional neural networks (ConvNets or CNNs)**, used by most computer vision applications, and focuses on image classification with **small training datasets**, the most common case for anyone outside a large tech company.

**Section 8.1** starts practically: before the theory, a simple ConvNet will classify **MNIST** digits, the task solved in chapter 2 with a dense network at **97.8% test accuracy**. Even this basic ConvNet will "blow out of the water" that result. The model is a stack of `Conv2D` and `MaxPooling2D` layers built with the **Functional API**.

**Listing 8.1** defines an input of shape `(28, 28, 1)`, then `Conv2D(64, 3, relu)` -> `MaxPooling2D(2)` -> `Conv2D(128, 3, relu)` -> `MaxPooling2D(2)` -> `Conv2D(256, 3, relu)` -> `GlobalAveragePooling2D()` -> `Dense(10, softmax)`, wrapped in `keras.Model(inputs=inputs, outputs=outputs)`. The resulting shapes and parameter counts are shown by `model.summary()` on p.257.

terminology.meaning: Layer that downsamples feature maps by taking maxima over windows; explained in 8.1.2 (p.263).

concepts.name: Convolutional neural network (ConvNet)
concepts.definition: A neural network built mainly from convolution and pooling layers, used by most computer vision applications.
concepts.intuition: Small learned pattern detectors scan the image; pooling summarizes their responses at coarser scales.
concepts.technical: Takes (height, width, channels) inputs (p.257) and produces feature maps whose spatial size shrinks and channel count grows with depth.
concepts.significance: Outperforms dense networks on images, starting with MNIST.
concepts.misconception: That ConvNets are only for large datasets; the chapter focuses on small ones.

concepts.name: Conv2D layer
concepts.definition: A layer that applies learned filters of size kernel_size over local windows of its input.
concepts.intuition: A small stencil slid over the image, computing a response at every position.
concepts.technical: filters sets the number of output channels; kernel_size=3 means 3x3 windows. Details from p.258.
concepts.misconception: That filters means the size of the window; it is the number of output channels (kernel_size is the window).

concepts.name: MaxPooling2D layer
concepts.definition: Downsampling layer that keeps the maximum value in each pool_size x pool_size window.
concepts.intuition: Keeps the strongest response in each neighbourhood, halving height and width with pool_size=2.
concepts.significance: Reduces spatial size and builds larger receptive fields.
concepts.misconception: That pooling has trainable weights; it has none.

concepts.name: GlobalAveragePooling2D
concepts.definition: Averages each channel over all spatial positions, turning (h, w, c) into a vector of length c.
concepts.intuition: One summary number per feature detector: how strongly, on average, did it fire across the image?
concepts.technical: In Listing 8.1 it turns the last (3, 3, 256) feature map into a 256-vector for the Dense classifier (shapes on p.257).
concepts.significance: Bridges convolutional features and a Dense classifier without a Flatten layer.
concepts.misconception: That it is the same as Flatten; Flatten keeps every value (3*3*256 = 2,304), global pooling averages to 256.

code.title: Instantiating a small ConvNet
code.original_code:
import keras
from keras import layers

inputs = keras.Input(shape=(28, 28, 1))
x = layers.Conv2D(filters=64, kernel_size=3, activation="relu")(inputs)
x = layers.MaxPooling2D(pool_size=2)(x)
x = layers.Conv2D(filters=128, kernel_size=3, activation="relu")(x)
x = layers.MaxPooling2D(pool_size=2)(x)
x = layers.Conv2D(filters=256, kernel_size=3, activation="relu")(x)
x = layers.GlobalAveragePooling2D()(x)
outputs = layers.Dense(10, activation="softmax")(x)
model = keras.Model(inputs=inputs, outputs=outputs)
code.what_it_does: Builds a small ConvNet for 28x28 grayscale digits with three convolution layers, two max-pooling layers, global average pooling and a 10-way softmax classifier.

line_explanations.explanation: Input tensor of shape (28, 28, 1): height, width and one grayscale channel (p.257).
64 learned 3x3 filters with ReLU; output (26, 26, 64) per the summary on p.257.
2x2 max pooling halves height and width: (13, 13, 64).
Averages each of the 256 channels over the 3x3 positions: vector of 256.
Dense softmax classifier over 10 digit classes.
Functional API model from inputs to outputs.

code.inputs_outputs: Input: batches of (28, 28, 1) images. Output: (batch, 10) class probabilities.
code.algorithm: Alternating convolution and pooling to extract increasingly abstract, spatially coarser features, followed by global pooling and a linear softmax classifier.

parameters.name: filters
parameters.role: Number of output channels (64, 128, 256): depth of the feature maps.

parameters.name: activation
parameters.role: ReLU in conv layers; softmax at the output.

pitfalls: MNIST from chapter 2 was flattened to (784,); for this model images must keep shape (28, 28, 1), with the channel axis.
The model is only defined here; it still needs compile() and fit().

deeper.title: Shape bookkeeping for Listing 8.1
deeper.body: Beyond the text on this page (the shapes are printed on p.257): a 3x3 convolution with no padding shrinks each side by 2 (28 -> 26), and 2x2 pooling halves it with floor rounding (26 -> 13, 11 -> 5). So: (28,28,1) -> (26,26,64) -> (13,13,64) -> (11,11,128) -> (5,5,128) -> (3,3,256) -> (256) -> (10).

deeper.title: Why the ConvNet should beat the dense model
deeper.body: Beyond the book (the theory follows on p.258): the dense chapter 2 model saw each image as an unordered vector of 784 pixels and had to learn every pattern separately at every position. A ConvNet reuses the same small filters at every location and keeps the 2-D layout, so it learns local patterns once and recognizes them anywhere.

misconceptions.claim: Deep learning won over computer vision researchers immediately after 2012.
misconceptions.correction: The authors say skepticism remained strong in 2013 and 2014 and dominance came in 2016.

misconceptions.claim: In Conv2D, filters=64 means a 64x64 window.
misconceptions.correction: filters is the number of output channels; the window size is kernel_size=3 (3x3).

misconceptions.claim: ConvNets are only useful to large tech companies with huge datasets.
misconceptions.correction: The chapter focuses precisely on small training datasets.

questions.answer: It averages each channel of the last feature map over all spatial positions, producing a 256-dimensional vector for the Dense classifier.
